## What happened

The remote branch `main` holds one or more commits that your local `main` does not hold. Someone pushed to `main` after your last fetch. Git refuses the push, because a push must be a fast-forward. A fast-forward means the remote commit is already an ancestor of your commit. It is not, so Git stops. You lose no work. Your commits stay safe in your local repository.

## First, look at the gap

1. Run `git fetch origin`. This updates your copy of the remote branch. It changes no local branch.
2. Run `git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main`. This lists the commits you do not have.
3. Run `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD`. This lists the commits you want to push.

Step 3 tells you which case you are in. An empty result means you are only behind. Then a plain `git pull` fast-forwards you, and you have nothing to push.

## Then choose one of two ways

**Rebase.** Use this when your commits are local only, and nobody else pulled them.

1. Run `git pull --rebase origin main`.
2. Run `git push`.

Git replays your commits on top of the remote commits. The history stays linear.

**Merge.** Use this when you already shared your commits, or when your team prefers merges.

1. Run `git pull origin main`.
2. Run `git push`.

Git writes a merge commit that joins the two lines of history.

## If the rebase stops on a conflict

1. Edit each conflicted file.
2. Run `git add <file>` for each one.
3. Run `git rebase --continue`.

To abandon the attempt, run `git rebase --abort`. That returns you to the state before step 1.

## Do not force the push

`git push --force` deletes the other person's commits from the remote. Do not use it here. Reserve `--force-with-lease` for a branch whose history you rewrote on purpose, and never use it on a shared `main`.
